name: X-37
tagline: The Boeing X-37 is an uncrewed, reusable spaceplane that launches on a rocket, stays in orbit for months or years, and lands on a runway. The X-37B version has flown eight missions for the US Air Force and Space Force since April 2010, and its longest flight lasted 908 days.
quickFacts: The X-37 began as a NASA programme in 1999 and moved to DARPA on 13th September 2004. The Air Force announced the X-37B on 17th November 2006, and it is run by the Air Force Rapid Capabilities Office with the Space Force. Two X-37B vehicles have been built.{{ref:wiki-x37}}
The first X-37B mission, OTV-1, launched on 22nd April 2010 on an Atlas V and landed on 3rd December 2010 after 224 days.{{ref:wiki-x37}}
OTV-6 launched on 17th May 2020 and landed on 12th November 2022 after 908 days, the longest X-37B flight. The design requirement was 270 days.{{ref:wiki-x37}}

OTV-7 launched on 28th December 2023 on a Falcon Heavy into a highly elliptical orbit. It planned aerobraking in October 2024 and landed at Vandenberg on 7th March 2025 after 434 days.{{ref:wiki-x37}}

OTV-8 launched on a Falcon 9 from Kennedy as USSF-36 on 21st August 2025, carrying laser communications equipment and what is described as the highest-performing quantum inertial sensor tested in space. No landing was found in the sources checked.{{ref:wiki-x37}}
Boeing has said that cost and budget information for the X-37 is not releasable. Estimates for the whole programme run to about US$2 billion, which is unconfirmed.{{ref:wiki-x37}}

specifications.specificationsNote: The X-37B is a spaceplane, so atmospheric speed, range and ceiling do not apply. Figures are from the Wikipedia page; the payload bay is 7 ft by 4 ft and payload mass is 227 kg. The engine is not specified in the sources checked; power comes from gallium arsenide solar cells and lithium-ion batteries. The vehicle was designed for 270 days in orbit and has demonstrated 908. Weight is given as about 11,000 lb at launch.

variants.desc: The atmospheric test vehicle, first glided freely on 7th April 2006. The landing ended in a runway overrun and minor damage. A captive carry flight had taken place on 21st June 2005.

The orbital version that flies for the Air Force and Space Force. Two have been built, flown on eight missions from 2010. It launches on an Atlas V, Falcon 9 or Falcon Heavy and lands on a runway at Vandenberg or Kennedy, carrying experiments in a small payload bay.

From OTV-6 in 2020 the vehicle flew with a service module to carry more experiments. OTV-6 released FalconSat-8 on about 28th May 2020 and carried a Naval Research Laboratory experiment, and OTV-8 flies with a service module and laser communications.

overview: The Boeing X-37 is an uncrewed spaceplane that launches on a rocket, flies in orbit for as long as its mission requires, and lands itself on a runway. It began as a NASA programme in 1999, moved to DARPA on 13th September 2004, and is run by the Air Force Rapid Capabilities Office with the Space Force. The Air Force announced the X-37B on 17th November 2006.{{ref:wiki-x37}}
Two X-37B vehicles have flown eight missions. Most of what they test is not published.{{ref:wiki-x37}}

sections.heading: Origins & Concept: From NASA to the Air Force
paragraphs: The X-37A flew first as an atmospheric test article. It made a captive carry flight on 21st June 2005 and its first free glide on 7th April 2006, ending in a runway overrun with minor damage. The orbital X-37B followed, with its first mission on 22nd April 2010.{{ref:wiki-x37}}

The vehicle is 29 ft 3 in long, with a 14 ft 11 in span and a launch weight of about 11,000 lb. It has a payload bay of 7 ft by 4 ft and carries a payload of 227 kg, with power from gallium arsenide solar cells and lithium-ion batteries.{{ref:wiki-x37}}

sections.heading: The Eight Missions
paragraphs: OTV-1 flew from 22nd April 2010 to 3rd December 2010, 224 days. OTV-2 flew from 5th March 2011 to 16th June 2012, 468 days. OTV-3 flew from 11th December 2012 to 17th October 2014, 674 days, and OTV-4 from 20th May 2015 to 7th May 2017, 717 days, with a Hall-effect thruster experiment.{{ref:wiki-x37}}

OTV-5, launched on 7th September 2017, was the first X-37B on a Falcon 9, flying a higher inclination with the ASETS-II experiment until 27th October 2019, 779 days. OTV-6 flew from 17th May 2020 to 12th November 2022, 908 days, the first with a service module. It released FalconSat-8 on about 28th May 2020. Day counts differ by one in some sources.{{ref:wiki-x37}}

OTV-7 was launched on a Falcon Heavy on 28th December 2023 into a highly elliptical orbit, planned aerobraking in October 2024, and landed at Vandenberg on 7th March 2025 after 434 days. OTV-8 launched as USSF-36 on a Falcon 9 from Kennedy on 21st August 2025.{{ref:wiki-x37}}

sections.heading: Landing Sites and Operations
paragraphs: The landing sites have been Vandenberg Runway 12 for OTV-1, 2, 3 and 7, Kennedy Space Center's Shuttle Landing Facility Runway 15 for OTV-4, and Runway 33 there for OTV-5 and 6. The cumulative time in orbit passed 4,200 days in the sources checked.{{ref:wiki-x37}}
OTV-8 carries laser communications equipment and a quantum inertial sensor described as the highest-performing yet tested in space, and flies a service module.{{ref:wiki-x37}}

sections.heading: Secrecy, Cost and Speculation
paragraphs: Boeing says cost and budget information for the X-37 is not releasable. Estimates run to about US$2 billion for the whole programme, with an additional US$1 billion in funding mentioned in recent legislation and a Falcon Heavy launch costing about US$150 million, and none of these is confirmed per vehicle.{{ref:wiki-x37}}
Speculation that the X-37B carries weapons has been denied by the Pentagon. The Chinese Shenlong spaceplane is often compared with it.{{ref:wiki-x37}}

accidentsAndIncidents.title: X-37A first free glide ends in runway overrun
accidentsAndIncidents.summary: The X-37A made its first free glide overran the runway on landing and suffered minor damage.
